title: MATKP Mini-Review: Thermogenesis
bodyHtml:
Thermogenesis refers to the process of heat production within adipose tissue, primarily through non-shivering mechanisms. This process is largely mediated by uncoupling protein 1 (UCP1) located in the mitochondria of brown and beige adipocytes. Upon activation (typically by β-adrenergic stimulation), UCP1 dissipates the mitochondrial proton gradient, diverting energy from ATP synthesis directly into heat generation [Cannon & Nedergaard, 2004].

Classic brown adipose tissue (BAT) is abundant in neonates and small mammals (e.g., rodents, shrews), playing a vital role in maintaining core body temperature. However, BAT largely regresses and becomes sparse in adult humans. Some species such as certain pigs naturally lack UCP1 expression. In many species including humans, dogs, and even some pig breeds, thermogenic beige adipocytes can emerge within white adipose tissue depots in response to stimuli like cold exposure or adrenergic activation [Liu et al., 2013].

Positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) using ¹⁸F-FDG is considered the gold standard for BAT detection in humans, but it has limitations as it primarily captures glucose uptake and may fail to detect non-glucose-fueled thermogenesis. More granular techniques like RNA sequencing and immunohistochemistry for UCP1 and mitochondrial markers offer better depot-level resolution, but large comparative datasets across species are scarce, and standardization of these methods across species remains a challenge. A significant gap in the field is the lack of standardized definitions and thresholds for classifying brown, beige, and white adipocytes across different species and experimental conditions. Cross-species atlases of thermogenic potential and standardized criteria for beige adipocytes are urgently needed to resolve biological variation and fully understand their functional significance in mammalian physiology.

Key References:

Cannon B, Nedergaard J. (2004). Physiol Rev, 84(1):277–359.

Liu X, et al. (2013). J Endocrinol, 216(3):R19–R29.
